title: Can you serialize/deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson/Gson, and what are the caveats?
shortTitle: Can you serialize/deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson/Gson, and what are the caveats?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, a sealed hierarchy can be serialized and deserialized with Jackson or Gson, but polymorphic deserialization requires type information to be present in the JSON so the library can pick the correct permitted subtype. Jackson supports this cleanly through `@JsonTypeInfo` and `@JsonSubTypes`, and modern Jackson can even infer permitted subtypes from the sealed `permits` list. Gson needs a registered `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` or a custom adapter because Gson has no built-in polymorphic support. The main caveats are embedding a type discriminator, keeping the registered or annotated subtype set in sync with the sealed `permits`, and handling records (common sealed leaves) which need constructor-based binding.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends account documents between systems as forms (JSON). Reading a form back is easy if the form has a clear label at the top saying which exact product it is — "Savings," "Current," or "Loan" — so the clerk knows which specific form template to use. Without that label, the clerk sees the fields but cannot be sure which product it is, and may fill in the wrong template. Serialization writes the form; deserialization reads it back; and the type label is the discriminator that tells the reader which permitted product to reconstruct.
s1_definition.oneliner: Yes — serialize freely, but polymorphic deserialization needs a type discriminator in the JSON, via Jackson's `@JsonTypeInfo`/`@JsonSubTypes` or Gson's `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, a sealed hierarchy can be serialized and deserialized with Jackson or Gson, but polymorphic deserialization requires type information to be present in the JSON so the library can pick the correct permitted subtype. Jackson supports this cleanly through `@JsonTypeInfo` and `@JsonSubTypes`, and modern Jackson can even infer permitted subtypes from the sealed `permits` list. Gson needs a registered `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` or a custom adapter because Gson has no built-in polymorphic support. The main caveats are embedding a type discriminator, keeping the registered or annotated subtype set in sync with the sealed `permits`, and handling records (common sealed leaves) which need constructor-based binding.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sends account documents between systems as forms (JSON). Reading a form back is easy if the form has a clear label at the top saying which exact product it is — "Savings," "Current," or "Loan" — so the clerk knows which specific form template to use. Without that label, the clerk sees the fields but cannot be sure which product it is, and may fill in the wrong template. Serialization writes the form; deserialization reads it back; and the type label is the discriminator that tells the reader which permitted product to reconstruct.

**One line to remember:** Yes — serialize freely, but polymorphic deserialization needs a type discriminator in the JSON, via Jackson's `@JsonTypeInfo`/`@JsonSubTypes` or Gson's `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory`.

sections.s2_technical:
**Serialization** (object to JSON) of a sealed hierarchy is straightforward because the library just reads the concrete object's fields. The challenge is **deserialization** (JSON back to object) when the declared type is the sealed supertype: the library receives JSON and must decide which permitted subtype to instantiate, and plain field data alone is often ambiguous. The solution is to include a **type discriminator** in the JSON — a property whose value names the subtype — so the library can route to the correct class.

In **Jackson**, you enable this with `@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, property = "type")` on the sealed type and `@JsonSubTypes` listing the mappings, for example `@JsonSubTypes.Type(value = SavingsAccount.class, name = "SAVINGS")`. Then JSON like `{"type":"SAVINGS","id":"SAV2001","balance":1000000}` deserializes into a `SavingsAccount`. A modern convenience is that recent Jackson versions can **infer the subtypes from the sealed `permits` clause**, reducing the need to list them manually, though you still choose the discriminator strategy. Jackson handles **records** well through their canonical constructor, which is important because sealed leaves are frequently records.

In **Gson**, there is **no built-in polymorphic deserialization**, so you must register a `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` (from the `gson-extras` companion) that maps a discriminator value to each subtype: `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory.of(Account.class, "type").registerSubtype(SavingsAccount.class, "SAVINGS")...`. You register it on the `GsonBuilder`. Without this, Gson deserializing into the sealed supertype cannot know the concrete type and fails or produces wrong results. Gson also does not natively bind to record canonical constructors in older versions, so records may need a custom adapter or a recent Gson release.

The **caveats** are the heart of the answer. First, you must **embed a discriminator** and agree on its name and values with every producer and consumer of the JSON. Second, the set of **subtypes known to the serializer must match the sealed `permits`**: if someone adds a permitted subtype but forgets to register or annotate it, deserialization of that new type fails at runtime — a gap the compiler cannot catch for the external JSON boundary. Third, **records as leaves** require constructor binding and have no setters, so the library must support canonical constructors. Fourth, **security**: never enable Jackson default typing that accepts arbitrary class names from JSON, because that is a well-known deserialization vulnerability; use the controlled `Id.NAME` mapping, which only permits your known subtypes — especially critical in banking.

A senior nuance is that sealing actually **helps** here conceptually, because the closed `permits` list is the exact, authoritative set the serializer must support, so you can derive or validate the registered subtypes against it, and Jackson's inference leans on this. Another nuance is **versioning**: when the JSON crosses service boundaries, adding a new permitted subtype is a wire-compatibility change that old consumers cannot deserialize, so you manage it like any schema evolution. A final nuance is that for internal, trusted JSON you can rely on Jackson's permits inference, but for external or cross-organisation JSON you keep an explicit, reviewed discriminator mapping to stay safe and stable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India sends account objects between microservices as JSON, and the receiving service declares the field as the sealed `Account` supertype. When it reads the JSON it must reconstruct the exact product. Without a type label the service cannot tell a savings account from a current account. We add a discriminator and configure Jackson to route correctly.

Problem 2 — A partner integration uses Gson instead of Jackson, which has no built-in polymorphic support, so the bank must register a `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` mapping the discriminator to each permitted subtype. We show that configuration.

Problem 3 — The bank wants safety: it must never allow arbitrary class names in incoming JSON to be instantiated, because that is a deserialization attack vector. We use controlled name-based mapping limited to the known permitted subtypes.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` with Jackson annotations and permitted record subtypes, serialize and deserialize with Jackson, then show the equivalent Gson `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` setup in a method, logging the round-trips.

The code contains: a sealed annotated `Account`, record subtypes, a Jackson round-trip, and a Gson round-trip configuration.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a `SavingsAccount` for SAV2001 with balance 1,000,000, declared through the sealed `Account` supertype.

Step 1 — Jackson serializes the savings account. Because the sealed `Account` carries `@JsonTypeInfo` with property `type` and `@JsonSubTypes` mapping `SavingsAccount` to the name `SAVINGS`, the output JSON includes `"type":"SAVINGS"` along with the id and balance fields.

Step 2 — Jackson deserializes that JSON back into the `Account` type. It reads the `type` property, finds the mapping to `SavingsAccount`, and binds the remaining fields through the record's canonical constructor, producing a `SavingsAccount` object. Logging confirms the concrete subtype, id, and balance.

Step 3 — The code shows the Gson configuration in comments: because Gson has no built-in polymorphism, a `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` maps the `type` discriminator to each permitted subtype and is registered on the `GsonBuilder`. With it, Gson round-trips the same way; without it, Gson cannot pick the subtype.

Step 4 — The security note explains that we rely on name-based mapping limited to the known permitted subtypes, and never enable Jackson default typing, which would allow attacker-controlled class names in JSON to be instantiated.

Step 5 — The caveats are summarised: the discriminator must be agreed by producers and consumers, the registered or annotated subtype set must stay in sync with the sealed `permits`, and record leaves bind through constructors.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SavingsAccount(SAV2001, 1,000,000) as Account
    │ Jackson writeValueAsString  (@JsonTypeInfo type=SAVINGS)
    ▼
  JSON: {"type":"SAVINGS","id":"SAV2001","balance":1000000}
    │ over the wire between services
    ▼
  Jackson readValue(json, Account.class)
    │ read "type"=SAVINGS → map to SavingsAccount (@JsonSubTypes)
    │ bind fields via record canonical constructor
    ▼
  SavingsAccount object reconstructed

  GSON path (no built-in polymorphism):
    GsonBuilder.registerTypeAdapterFactory(
      RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory.of(Account, "type")
        .registerSubtype(SavingsAccount,"SAVINGS") ... )
    toJson / fromJson round-trip via the factory

  SECURITY: Id.NAME mapping only → no arbitrary class instantiation
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, I can serialize and deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson or Gson, but the real work is in polymorphic deserialization, because when the declared type is the sealed supertype the library must decide which permitted subtype to build, and the plain field data is often ambiguous. The solution is to embed a type discriminator in the JSON, a property whose value names the subtype, so the library can route to the correct class.

With Jackson I put JsonTypeInfo using the name strategy and a type property on the sealed type, and JsonSubTypes listing each subtype name mapping. Then JSON that carries type equals savings deserializes into my savings account. Modern Jackson can even infer the subtypes from the sealed permits clause, which is convenient, and it binds record leaves through their canonical constructor, which matters because sealed leaves are so often records. With Gson there is no built-in polymorphic support, so I register a runtime type adapter factory that maps the discriminator value to each permitted subtype and add it to the Gson builder; without it Gson cannot pick the concrete type.

The caveats are what I emphasise. First, I must embed and agree the discriminator name and values across every producer and consumer. Second, the subtype set known to the serializer must stay in sync with the sealed permits, because if someone adds a permitted subtype but forgets to register or annotate it, deserialization of that new type fails at runtime, and the compiler cannot catch that at the external JSON boundary. Third, records as leaves need constructor binding since they have no setters. Fourth, and most important in a bank, security: I never enable Jackson default typing on untrusted JSON, because accepting arbitrary class names is a classic deserialization attack; I use the controlled name mapping that only permits my known subtypes.

What I like to add is that sealing actually helps here, because the closed permits list is the authoritative set the serializer must support, so I can derive or validate the registered subtypes against it, which is exactly what Jackson's inference relies on. The one thing I manage carefully is versioning across service boundaries, because adding a new permitted subtype is a wire-compatibility change that old consumers cannot read, so I treat it like any schema evolution with a registry and compatibility rules. So the answer is yes, with a discriminator, with the subtype mapping kept in sync with permits, and with default typing kept firmly off.

---

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
